summary: Caisson light on Wolf Trap Shoal in the lower Chesapeake Bay, built in 1894 after ice carried off the 1870 screw-pile light; private and not open to the public.

lens.note: Fourth-order lantern per the 1894 engineer's report; the archive dates the original lens to 1897; the current optic is a solar-powered VRB-25.

structures.material: brick dwelling on a cast-iron shell pier over a wooden caisson

access.note: Not open to the public (USLHS record). Privately owned.

facts.agency: Private owner (Richard Cuce, with The Lighthouse Centers, per the USLHS record)

events.note: Lightship stationed on Wolf Trap Shoal (chapter timeline; the archive gives 1821 as establishment)
Lightship destroyed by Confederate troops (chapter timeline)
Screw-pile light on iron piles; the 1894 report calls it an iron skeleton structure, the Board's narrative a wooden building on iron screw piles
Carried away by ice on 22 January 1893

House floated and was towed toward the south shore (Richmond Dispatch); the Board's report says apparatus was recovered and stored at the Portsmouth depot; the chapter timeline says the lighthouse was swept 20 miles down the bay and settled near Thimble Shoal.
Temporary gas buoy in March; tender Holly moored as a temporary light-vessel from 30 June
Light-vessel No. 46 at Wolf Trap Shoal: boiler explosion on 28 August 1893 killed the engineer in charge and one seaman
Present brick dwelling on cast-iron pier; pier completed April 1894
Schooner Dorothy Palmer runs aground at the light (chapter timeline)
Schooner Cary Ann Bell sinks near the light (chapter timeline)
Assistant keeper John Morgan rescues crew of a disabled plane (chapter timeline)
Keeper and assistant aid a family of six stranded by a storm (chapter timeline)
Automation (chapter timeline); the archive roster ends in 1971
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places (02001434), 2 December 2002
Sold at auction after being made available for ownership in 2004-2005 (chapter timeline)
Coast Guard declares the light unsafe for personnel to access and maintain; light discontinued (chapter timeline). The archive still lists it as an active aid.
Purchased by Richard Cuce (chapter timeline; USLHS owner field)

corrections.why: The chapter timeline dates automation to 1971, and the archive roster's last keeper stint ends in 1971.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sources give different first years because they name different structures: a lightship on the shoal from 1821, a screw-pile light from 1870, and the present caisson light built in 1894.

notes_for_editor: Richmond Dispatch and Richmond Times, 22 January 1893: the Times account of a keeper (William Gunter) who abandoned the light after ice damaged the lens concerns the Old Plantation Flats light, a separate station in the Chesapeake. The Lighthouse Board's own 1893 report lists Old Plantation Flats separately. It is not used here. Keeper in January 1893: the Roanoke interview names John William Thomas as assistant keeper. The archive roster starts in 1894, so the 1893 keepers are not on it. Roanoke gives the old site as twelve feet of water and three miles from shore; the story does not use that. The 1870 structure: Bergland calls it an iron skeleton structure; the Board's 1894 narrative calls it a wooden building on iron screw piles. Both are quoted. The wreck has three accounts: the Board (apparatus recovered from the floating wreck and stored at Portsmouth), the Richmond Dispatch (a revenue cutter towed it to the south shore) and the chapter timeline (swept 20 miles down the bay, settling near Thimble Shoal). The Dispatch OCR reads 'Mornll' for the cutter's name; not named in the story. Bergland's distances are OCR'd with garbled fraction signs ('12|' and '1\' miles); the story says about 12 miles and under two miles rather than guess the fractions. Bergland's report is dated 11 September 1894 (Baltimore). Tradition of the name: the Roanoke article gives the British man-of-war Wolf 'during the revolution'; Wikipedia gives 1691, which is not cited because Wikipedia is leads only. Lens: the timeline says 4th-order in 1894; the USLHS record gives an original lens year of 1897. Left open. Automation: the record says 2007; the chapter timeline and the roster end both point to 1971 (see corrections). Last civilian keeper: the timeline says Crewe retired in 1968 after 38 years as the last Lighthouse Service civilian keeper and dates his start to 1954; the roster gives him as first assistant 1954-1956 and principal 1956-1968. Morgan: the timeline's 'Assistant Keeper John Morgan' has no middle initial; the roster's only Morgan is John E. Morgan; the story does not link them. Status: the timeline says discontinued in 2017; the USLHS record still shows an active aid. Left open in the story. Light characteristic: the Board's list of changed lights records a change on 28 February 1896 from a fixed light with a flash every 10 seconds to one with a flash every 25 seconds (1895 volume, annualreportlig00boargoog). Not in the story. Wikipedia dates the change to 1895. Owner: the USLHS record and the timeline name the current owner, a private individual with The Lighthouse Centers; the story does not name him. Earlier private owners are not named. The 1894 date of first light is not confirmed by a source read; the story says the present structure was built in 1894 and gives no first-lit date for it. Keepers counted: 114 stints (roster.py; 55 under the USCG heading). Names matched by column position: none.
